papers.title: Rosewood-Derived Hard Carbon with a Tailored Microstructure as a High-Performance Anode for Sodium-Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: Abstract Biomass-derived hard carbon has attracted extensive attention as a sustainable anode material for sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), yet simultaneously achieving high initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) and large low-voltage plateau capacity remains challenging because both are strongly governed by carbon microstructure evolution during pyrolysis. Herein, waste rosewood is regulated through time-controlled alkaline treatment combined with multistage carbonization to balance surface stabilization and internal structural evolution. Moderate hemicellulose removal suppresses disordered surface defects and oxygen-rich unstable sites, leading to a compact carbon surface with reduced irreversible sodium consumption. Meanwhile, multistage carbonization promotes graphitic rearrangement and internal nanopore development for plateau sodium storage. Consequently, AMHC-5 delivers a reversible capacity of 325.2 mAh g−1 with an ICE of 90.0% at 0.1 A g−1 and a plateau capacity of 219.6 mAh g−1. Electrochemical measurements and in situ Raman and impedance analyses reveal sequential sodium storage involving adsorption, intercalation, and pore filling. A full cell paired with Na3V2(PO4)3 retains 85.6% of its capacity after 100 cycles. This work clarifies the relationship between precursor composition, carbon evolution, and sodium-storage behavior, offering a simple route for designing advanced biomass-derived hard carbon anodes for SIBs.

papers.title: Tailoring Microstructure of Lignin-Derived Hard Carbon Nanofibers via Molecular Stitching for Enhanced Sodium-Ion Storage
papers.abstract: Abstract Renewable lignin is an attractive biomass precursor for sustainable hard carbon in sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) owing to its renewability, high carbon yield, and intrinsically molecular disordered structure. However, severe structural collapse during carbonization and low initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) hinder its practical application. Herein, an integrated strategy of PMDA-mediated molecular stitching and electrospinning with PVP as a fiber-forming aid was used to fabricate binder-free, self-supporting lignin-derived carbon nanofibers (LCNFs). With an optical PMDA content of 10 wt %, LCNF-P10 forms a robust three-dimensional cross-linked network through in situ esterification, effectively suppressing structural collapse during carbonization. Meanwhile, the synergistic effect of molecular stitching and PVP-derived pore engineering generates a highly disordered carbon framework with enlarged interlayer spacing (0.381 nm), hierarchical porosity, and abundant closed nanopores, thereby promoting low-voltage sodium storage. Consequently, LCNF-P10 delivers a high reversible capacity of 374.7 mAh g–1, an exceptional ICE of 89.39%, good rate capability, and excellent long-term cycling stability. The full cell assembled with a Na3V2(PO4)3 cathode achieves a high energy density of 240 Wh kg–1. This work demonstrates a sustainable molecular engineering strategy for converting renewable lignin into high-performance, freestanding hard carbon electrodes, providing new insights into the scalable utilization of biomass resources for practical sodium-ion batteries.

papers.title: Programming Closed Pores in Hard Carbon Anodes via Alcohol‐Regulated Interfacial Assembly for High‐Rate and Durable Sodium‐Ion Storage
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Closed pores are widely recognized as the primary structural domains responsible for the low‐voltage plateau capacity of hard carbon anodes for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). However, current strategies for constructing closed pores predominantly rely on post‐carbonization reconstruction, offering limited control over pore accessibility and interfacial chemistry. Here we demonstrate that closed pores can instead be programmed during the precursor assembly process via an alcohol‐regulated interfacial assembly strategy. By systematically modulating the alcohol/water solvent environment, hydrogen‐bond interactions, micelle swelling behavior, and pyrrole polymerization kinetics are cooperatively regulated, enabling programmable precursor confinement and the subsequent transformation of micelle‐pyrrole assemblies into closed‐pore‐rich hard carbons during carbonization. The optimized hard carbon exhibits abundant closed ultramicropores that not only facilitate the quasi‐metallic sodium cluster filling but also promote the formation of a thin inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, thereby accelerating sodium‐storage kinetics. As a result, it delivers an outstanding rate capability of 119 mAh g −1 at 10 A g −1 and robust cycling stability over 6000 cycles at 5 A g −1 , as well as excellent low‐temperature performance at −20°C. This work establishes precursor organization programming as a general strategy for constructing closed pores in hard carbon materials toward fast‐charging and long‐life SIBs.

papers.title: Hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries: from mechanistic reconciliation, precursor-tailored microstructure regulation to industrial scale-up
papers.abstract: Hard carbon is the leading anode candidate for sodium-ion batteries, yet its practical deployment remains constrained by three interconnected gaps: the sodium storage mechanism is disputed across competing models, no precursor classification framework links chemical composition to electrochemical function, and predictive structure–property relationships remain largely empirical. This review traces the precursor-to-performance pipeline. We show that the insertion-filling, adsorption-insertion, and adsorption-filling models converge on a multi-stage adsorption-intercalation-filling paradigm, where the intercalation-to-filling balance is governed by carbonization temperature, precursor chemistry, and pore architecture rather than by a single mechanism. We then introduce a three-dimensional precursor classification framework—spanning scalability, structural controllability, and performance ceiling—and deconvolute the component-specific pyrolysis pathways of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin to establish how molecular architecture is transmitted into carbon microstructure. Three microstructure engineering levers are critically evaluated: pore-structure manipulation to resolve the low-surface-area/high-closed-pore-volume trade-off, interlayer-spacing regulation via heteroatom doping and pre-oxidation, and defect engineering guided by the conductivity-capacity Pareto Frontier. The rapid industrialization of hard carbon—from laboratory discovery to 10,000-ton-scale manufacturing—is assessed, documenting how precursor diversification and process innovation have driven costs toward parity with graphite anodes. Finally, the current challenges and future development directions of high-performance and industrializable hard carbon anodes are prospected, aiming to provide systematic theoretical guidance and technical references for the further design, modification and large-scale application of hard carbon materials in advanced sodium-ion batteries.

papers.title: Revealing the closed pore formation of waste wood-derived hard carbon for advanced sodium-ion battery
papers.abstract: Abstract Although the closed pore structure plays a key role in contributing low-voltage plateau capacity of hard carbon anode for sodium-ion batteries, the formation mechanism of closed pores is still under debate. Here, we employ waste wood-derived hard carbon as a template to systematically establish the formation mechanisms of closed pores and their effect on sodium storage performance. We find that the high crystallinity cellulose in nature wood decomposes to long-range carbon layers as the wall of closed pore, and the amorphous component can hinder the graphitization of carbon layer and induce the crispation of long-range carbon layers. The optimized sample demonstrates a high reversible capacity of 430 mAh g −1 at 20 mA g −1 (plateau capacity of 293 mAh g −1 for the second cycle), as well as good rate and stable cycling performances (85.4% after 400 cycles at 500 mA g −1 ). Deep insights into the closed pore formation will greatly forward the rational design of hard carbon anode with high capacity.
